title: A blessing at every meal
hook: one blessing before, one thanks after
tomorrow: a little box with a slot sits in the kitchen. what goes in it?

segments.voice: Two weeks: the later voices closed, and you added yours. Then a rule of three lines, Modeh Ani on waking, water over each hand, and yesterday, the morning Shema, eyes covered, listening first. Hear, every morning. Today, the meals in between, and then the recent lines come back as a game.

Lunch eaten standing at the counter, one hand on the sandwich, the other scrolling. Done in minutes, forgotten by dinner. Nobody at that counter is doing anything wrong; the food just came and went without anyone noticing it arrive. Jewish tradition puts a small frame around every meal: one blessing before, and a thank-you after. The one before is easy to remember; you're hungry. So why does the Torah ask for one after?
screen: `LUNCH AT THE COUNTER.` → `ONE BEFORE, ONE AFTER.` → `WHY THE ONE AFTER?`

segments.voice: Because full is when you forget. Deuteronomy puts it plainly: "And thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God for the good land which He hath given thee." Eat, be satisfied, then bless. The very next verses warn against forgetting once you've eaten your fill. That's the root of the grace after meals, the thank-you said when the plate is empty. Look at what it thanks God for: the good land, not just lunch. When the plate is empty, the thank-you reaches past the plate. The blessing before is the rabbis' addition. The Talmud teaches that enjoying anything of this world without a blessing is like taking without asking. So before bread, Jews say hamotzi: blessed are You, who brings forth bread from the earth. Notice the picture: not bread from a bakery, but from the earth, as if the whole chain, soil, rain, farmer, baker, is being thanked at once. Other foods have their own short blessings too, for fruit, for wine, for everything else, so no snack falls outside the frame. One frame, two edges. Hungry, you remember; full, you remember again. And every meal in between is blessed.
screen: `FULL IS WHEN YOU FORGET.` · `EAT, BE SATISFIED, BLESS.` · `HAMOTZI: BREAD FROM THE EARTH.` · then, large: `EVERY MEAL BLESSED.`

segments.voice: If you have something to eat or drink nearby, take one small bite or sip, slowly, and taste it all the way through, the way you would taste something for the first time. If you say blessings, say the one before; if not, name one person in the chain that brought it to you. When it's gone, say a short thank-you, out loud, for being satisfied, and notice that you are.
screen: `ONE SLOW BITE.` · `A BLESSING, OR ONE NAME IN THE CHAIN.` · `THANKS WHEN IT'S GONE.`

segments.voice: A blessing at every meal: hamotzi before bread, and grace after, from Deuteronomy's eat, be satisfied, and bless. A frame around every meal, so that none of them simply disappears.
screen: `A BLESSING AT EVERY MEAL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Keep it close: every meal blessed, hungry and full. Two weeks, done; the game round's next.

howItsDone: Before eating bread, Jews say hamotzi, and after a meal with bread, Birkat Hamazon, the grace after meals, sometimes sung together at the table; other foods have their own short blessings before and after.

fork.setup: the holiday meal is over, everyone's stuffed, and the kids are already heading for the couch. by Deuteronomy, which moment needs the blessing most?

the start only, since thanks counts most when you're hungry.

fork.reveal: eat, be satisfied, and bless: the Torah's blessing comes when you're full, and the next verses warn against forgetting.

chat.says: first dinner with Hana. she said bismillah, i said hamotzi, then we both just laughed. is that weird?
options: Not weird. Two blessings at one table; each of you thanked God in your own words.
A bit. At a shared table it's better to pick one blessing so nobody feels left out.
Yes. Blessings are private, so saying them out loud with a roommate is too much.
chat.meaning: Jews bless food before and after; Muslims say bismillah, in the name of God, before eating. Shared gratitude, each in its own words.

notes: Deuteronomy 8:10 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm exact wording. 8:11–12 paraphrased.

'The blessing before is the rabbis' addition': the blessing after (Birkat Hamazon) is Torah-level, blessings before eating rabbinic (Berakhot 35a, 21a); confirm phrasing. Berakhot 35a's 'like taking without asking' paraphrases 'as if he benefited from consecrated property' / 'as if he robbed'; confirm the softened image.
